question: Why does the manual say night driving is more dangerous than daytime driving?
choice_a: Drivers can't see hazards as quickly and have less time to respond
choice_b: Speed limits are always higher at night
choice_c: Traffic laws are different at night
choice_d: Vehicles are mechanically less reliable at night
explanation: The manual states drivers can't see hazards as quickly as in daylight, so they have less time to respond, making night driving riskier.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.1, It's More Dangerous

question: Even a two-second period of glare blindness at 55 mph can cause a vehicle to travel about how far?
choice_a: More than half the length of a football field
choice_b: A few feet
choice_c: Less than a car length
choice_d: About one mile
explanation: The manual states a vehicle going 55 mph will travel more than half the distance of a football field during two seconds of glare blindness.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2, Glare

question: According to the manual, most people are less alert at night, especially:
choice_a: Only when it is raining
choice_b: Right after sunset
choice_c: During the morning commute
choice_d: Especially after midnight
explanation: The manual states most people are less alert at night, especially after midnight.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2, Fatigue and Lack of Alertness

question: When should you be especially alert for drunk drivers, according to the manual's discussion of roadway factors at night?
choice_a: Right after sunrise
choice_b: Around the closing times for bars and taverns
choice_c: Only during holiday weekends
choice_d: Only in residential areas
explanation: The manual advises being especially alert around the closing times for bars and taverns for drunk drivers.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.3, Drunk Drivers

question: About how far ahead can you see with low-beam headlights, according to the manual?
choice_a: About 500 feet
choice_b: About 750 feet
choice_c: About 100 feet
choice_d: About 250 feet
explanation: The manual states you can see ahead about 250 feet with low beams.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.4, Headlights

question: About how far ahead can you see with high-beam headlights, according to the manual?
explanation: The manual states you can see about 350-500 feet ahead with high beams.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.4, Headlights

question: Within what distance of an oncoming or followed vehicle should you dim your headlights at night?
choice_a: 1,000 feet
choice_b: 250 feet
choice_c: 100 feet
choice_d: 500 feet
explanation: The manual instructs dimming your lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when following another vehicle within 500 feet.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.5, Avoid Blinding Others

question: If an oncoming driver fails to dim their high beams, what does the manual advise you to do?
choice_a: Pull off the road immediately and stop
choice_b: Do not try to "get back at them" by switching to your own high beams
choice_c: Honk your horn continuously until they dim their lights
choice_d: Flash your own high beams back at them repeatedly
explanation: The manual advises not retaliating with your own high beams, since this increases glare for oncoming drivers and the chance of a crash.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.5, Avoid Glare from Oncoming Vehicles

question: What is the only safe cure for sleepiness while driving, according to the manual?
choice_a: Turning on the radio loudly
choice_b: Opening a window for fresh air
choice_c: Sleep, by stopping at the nearest safe place
choice_d: Drinking coffee or another caffeinated beverage
explanation: The manual states that if you are sleepy, the only safe cure is to get off the road and get some sleep.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.5, If You Get Sleepy, Stop at the Nearest Safe Place

question: According to the manual, why should you avoid keeping the cab's interior light on at night while using high beams?
choice_a: It makes it harder to see outside the vehicle
choice_b: It is against motor carrier policy everywhere
choice_c: It interferes with the ABS system
choice_d: It drains the battery too quickly
explanation: The manual advises keeping the interior light off and instrument lights low, because a bright cab interior makes it harder to see outside.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.5, Use High Beams When You Can

question: What is the manual's best overall advice for driving in fog?
choice_a: Drive slightly faster to clear the fog bank quickly
choice_b: Follow closely behind another vehicle's taillights
choice_c: Don't drive in fog; pull off the road until visibility improves
choice_d: Use high-beam headlights for maximum visibility
explanation: The manual states the best advice for driving in fog is don't, and to pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility is better.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12, Driving in Fog

question: If you must drive in fog, which headlight setting does the manual recommend, even in daytime?
choice_a: High beams for maximum range
choice_b: Low-beam headlights and fog lights
choice_c: Parking lights only
choice_d: No lights, to avoid glare off the fog
explanation: The manual recommends using low-beam headlights and fog lights for best visibility even in daytime fog.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12, Driving in Fog

question: Seeing taillights or headlights ahead of you in fog may not reliably indicate:
choice_a: The speed of the vehicle ahead
choice_b: Where the road actually is, since that vehicle may not be on the road at all
choice_c: That fog lights are legal in your state
choice_d: That another vehicle is present
explanation: The manual warns that seeing taillights or headlights ahead may not be a true indication of where the road is, since that vehicle may not be on the road at all.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12, Driving in Fog

question: Which of the following does the manual specifically advise against while driving in fog?
choice_a: Turning on your four-way flashers
choice_b: Passing other vehicles
choice_c: Listening for traffic you cannot see
choice_d: Using roadside reflectors as a guide to the road's curve
explanation: The manual specifically advises avoiding passing other vehicles while driving in fog.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12, Driving in Fog

question: According to the manual, why should you carefully inspect tire chains before winter driving?
choice_a: Chains improve fuel economy in the winter
choice_b: You may find yourself unable to drive without chains, even to reach a place of safety
choice_c: Chains are required only for passenger cars
choice_d: Chains are only needed for decoration
explanation: The manual explains that in some winter conditions you can't drive without chains, even to get to a place of safety, so they must be carried and checked.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.1, Tire Chains

question: Why are exhaust system leaks especially dangerous in winter?
choice_a: They cause the engine to overheat immediately
choice_b: They make the exhaust louder, distracting the driver
choice_c: They can let poisonous carbon monoxide leak into the vehicle when ventilation is poor
choice_d: They reduce fuel economy significantly
explanation: The manual warns that exhaust leaks are especially dangerous when cab ventilation is poor, such as with windows rolled up, since carbon monoxide can leak in and cause drowsiness or death.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.1, Exhaust System

question: What is one way to check for ice on the road, according to the manual?
choice_a: Ice only forms when the temperature is below 0 degrees Fahrenheit
choice_b: A lack of spray from other vehicles indicates ice has formed
choice_c: Ice never forms on bridges before the rest of the road
choice_d: Check only the vehicle's fuel gauge
explanation: The manual states that a lack of spray from other vehicles indicates ice has formed on the road.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2, Check for Ice

question: Why does the manual advise against using the engine brake or speed retarder on slippery winter roads?
choice_a: They can cause the driving wheels to skid on slippery surfaces
choice_b: They use more fuel than regular braking
choice_c: They are illegal to use below freezing
choice_d: They wear out faster in cold weather
explanation: The manual states not to use the engine brake or speed retarder on slippery roads because they can cause the driving wheels to skid.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2, Adjust Turning and Braking to Conditions

question: After driving through deep standing water, what should you do to dry out wet brakes?
choice_a: Stop immediately and disconnect the brake lines
choice_b: Accelerate hard with the brakes fully released
choice_c: Maintain light pressure on the brakes for a short distance to heat them and dry them out
choice_d: Shift into neutral and coast until they dry naturally
explanation: The manual instructs maintaining light brake pressure for a short distance after driving through water to heat the brakes and dry them out, then making a test stop.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2, Wet Brakes

question: As temperature rises toward the point where ice begins to melt, what happens to the road, according to the manual?
choice_a: It becomes safer and less slippery
choice_b: It only affects tire pressure, not traction
choice_c: It becomes even more slippery
choice_d: There is no change in traction
explanation: The manual warns that as ice begins to melt, the road becomes even more slippery, so you should slow down more.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2, Adjust Speed to Conditions

question: How often does the manual recommend inspecting tires when driving in very hot weather?
choice_a: Only at the start and end of the trip
choice_b: Every four hours or every 200 miles
choice_c: Every hour or every 50 miles
choice_d: Every two hours or every 100 miles
explanation: The manual recommends inspecting tires every two hours or every 100 miles when driving in very hot weather.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1, Tires

question: If a tire is too hot to touch during hot weather driving, what should you do?
choice_a: Add more air pressure immediately
choice_b: Let air out of the tire until it cools
choice_c: Continue driving slowly to help it cool faster
choice_d: Remain stopped until the tire cools off
explanation: The manual instructs remaining stopped until an overly hot tire cools off, since otherwise it may blow out or catch fire.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1, Tires

question: When should you never remove the radiator cap or any part of the pressurized cooling system?
choice_a: Only when the engine is running
choice_b: Radiator caps can always be removed safely
choice_c: Until the system has cooled
choice_d: Only when the vehicle is parked on an incline
explanation: The manual warns never to remove the radiator cap or pressurized system parts until the system has cooled, since steam and boiling water can spray under pressure and cause severe burns.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1, Engine Coolant

question: What road hazard does the manual warn about, caused by pavement tar rising to the surface in very hot weather?
choice_a: Tar causes tires to overinflate
choice_b: Tar interferes with radio reception
choice_c: Bleeding tar creates very slippery spots
choice_d: Tar blocks the vehicle's air intake
explanation: The manual states that tar bleeding to the surface in hot weather creates spots that are very slippery.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.2, Driving

question: What distinguishes a "passive" railroad crossing from an "active" one, according to the manual?
choice_a: Passive crossings are always found on divided highways
choice_b: A passive crossing has no traffic control device, leaving the decision to stop entirely to the driver
choice_c: Passive crossings have gates; active crossings do not
choice_d: Active crossings are found only in rural areas
explanation: The manual defines a passive crossing as one with no traffic control device, where the decision to stop or proceed rests entirely with the driver.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.1, Types of Crossings

question: What should you do when the flashing red lights at a railroad crossing begin to flash?
choice_a: Sound your horn and continue driving
choice_b: Proceed cautiously if no train is visible
choice_c: Speed up to cross before the train arrives
choice_d: Stop, since a train is approaching and you must yield the right-of-way
explanation: The manual states that when the flashing red lights begin to flash, you must stop, since a train is approaching and you are required to yield the right-of-way.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.2, Flashing Red Light Signals

question: Why does the manual say a driver should never attempt to race a train to a crossing?
choice_a: Trains never travel faster than 20 mph
choice_b: It is only illegal at night
choice_c: It is difficult to judge the speed of an approaching train
choice_d: Racing a train is only a hazard for buses
explanation: The manual states it is extremely difficult to judge the speed of an approaching train, so you should never try to race one to a crossing.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.3, Driving Procedures

question: Why does the manual warn drivers to be extra careful at crossings with double tracks?
choice_a: Double-track crossings never have warning signs
choice_b: Double tracks are only found in cities
choice_c: A train on one track may hide a train approaching on the other track
choice_d: Trains on double tracks always travel side by side
explanation: The manual warns that a train on one track may hide a train on the other, so you should look both ways and double-check after one train clears.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.3, Double Tracks Require a Double Check

question: About how long does it take a typical tractor-trailer unit to clear a single railroad track?
choice_a: At least 5 seconds
choice_b: At least 40 seconds
choice_c: At least 25 seconds
choice_d: At least 14 seconds
explanation: The manual states it takes a typical tractor-trailer unit at least 14 seconds to clear a single track.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.5, Crossing the Tracks

question: According to the manual, what should you do with the gears while crossing railroad tracks?
choice_a: Do not shift gears while crossing
choice_b: Shift up one gear for extra clearance
choice_c: Shift into neutral to coast across
choice_d: Shift into the lowest gear available
explanation: The manual instructs drivers not to shift gears while crossing railroad tracks.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.5, Crossing the Tracks

question: Which type of trailer does the manual specifically warn can get stuck on raised railroad crossings?
choice_a: A tandem-axle flatbed
choice_b: A low-slung unit, such as a lowboy or car carrier
choice_c: A standard dry van trailer
choice_d: A refrigerated trailer
explanation: The manual lists low-slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers as at risk of getting stuck on raised crossings.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.6, Special Situations

question: If your vehicle gets stuck on the tracks at a railroad crossing, what does the manual instruct you to do first?
choice_a: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911
choice_b: Honk the horn continuously until help arrives
choice_c: Try to free the vehicle by rocking it forward and backward
choice_d: Stay in the vehicle and wait for the train to pass
explanation: The manual instructs getting out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then calling 911 or another emergency number and reporting the location.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.6, Special Situations

question: Why must you select the right, low gear before starting down a long, steep grade rather than after your speed has built up?
choice_a: You will not be able to shift into a lower gear once speed has built up, and could lose all engine braking effect
choice_b: State law requires a specific gear at the top of every grade
choice_c: It has no real safety effect either way
choice_d: It is only a fuel economy concern
explanation: The manual warns that you will not be able to downshift after speed has built up and may lose all engine braking effect, and could even damage an automatic transmission by forcing it into a lower gear at high speed.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.2, Select the Right Gear Before Starting Down the Grade

question: What is "brake fade," as described in the mountain driving section of the manual?
choice_a: A brake pedal that feels too stiff to press
choice_b: A feature that automatically reduces brake noise
choice_c: A gradual loss of stopping power from applying the brakes harder and harder due to overheating
choice_d: A cosmetic wearing of the brake pedal pad
explanation: The manual explains that when brakes get too hot they may start to fade, requiring harder and harder application for the same stopping power, until they may not stop the vehicle at all.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16, Mountain Driving

question: In the manual's proper downgrade braking technique, once you apply the brakes hard enough to feel a definite slowdown, when should you release them?
choice_a: When your speed has dropped to about 5 mph below your "safe" speed
choice_b: Immediately, after less than one second
choice_c: Only after coming to a complete stop
choice_d: Never release the brakes until reaching the bottom of the grade
explanation: The manual's technique is to apply the brakes until speed drops to about 5 mph below the safe speed, then release, repeating as needed.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.4, Proper Braking Technique

question: What are escape ramps designed to do, according to the manual?
choice_a: Allow vehicles to bypass weigh stations
choice_b: Stop runaway vehicles safely, often using a bed of loose, soft material
choice_c: Recharge a vehicle's air brake system
choice_d: Provide a faster route down a mountain
explanation: The manual describes escape ramps as using a long bed of loose, soft material, sometimes combined with an upgrade, to safely stop runaway vehicles.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.4, Proper Braking Technique

question: According to the manual, why is stopping not always the safest response in an emergency?
choice_a: You can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop
choice_b: Stopping always causes a rear-end collision
choice_c: Stopping is illegal on most highways
choice_d: Brakes are unreliable in every commercial vehicle
explanation: The manual notes that when you don't have enough room to stop, you may have to steer away, since you can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.1, Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: Why should you avoid applying the brake while making an emergency turn?
choice_a: It automatically disengages the transmission
choice_b: It is easy to lock the wheels while turning, which could cause a skid
choice_c: It has no significant effect either way
choice_d: It wastes brake fluid
explanation: The manual warns that braking while turning makes it easy to lock the wheels, which can cause you to skid out of control.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.1, How to Turn Quickly and Safely

question: What is "countersteering," as described in the manual's emergency steering guidance?
choice_a: A type of automatic stability control
choice_b: Steering with only one hand
choice_c: Turning the wheel back in the other direction once you've passed the obstacle
choice_d: Braking and steering at the same time
explanation: The manual describes countersteering as turning the wheel back in the other direction once you've passed whatever was in your path, as part of one continuous steering action.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.1, How to Turn Quickly and Safely

question: If you are blocked on both sides and must choose a direction to steer in an emergency, which does the manual generally recommend?
choice_a: A move to the left, toward the center of the road
choice_b: You should always stop instead of steering
choice_c: A move to the right, so you don't force anyone into an opposing traffic lane
choice_d: It makes no difference which way you steer
explanation: The manual states that if blocked on both sides, a move to the right may be best, since it avoids forcing anyone into oncoming traffic.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.1, Where to Steer

question: If you are forced to leave the road in an emergency, what does the manual advise regarding braking?
choice_a: Brake hard immediately upon leaving the pavement
choice_b: Never brake at all until you stop completely
choice_c: Avoid using the brakes until your speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then brake gently
choice_d: Apply the parking brake immediately
explanation: The manual advises avoiding braking until your speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then braking very gently to avoid skidding on the loose surface.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.1, Leaving the Road

question: When returning to the road after driving on the shoulder, why does the manual warn against edging back gradually?
choice_a: It is illegal in most states
choice_b: Your tires might grab unexpectedly and you could lose control
choice_c: It damages the shoulder surface
choice_d: It takes too much time
explanation: The manual warns that edging back gradually risks the tires grabbing unexpectedly, causing loss of control; instead, turn sharply and countersteer immediately.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.1, Returning to the Road

question: In the "controlled braking" method for stopping quickly, what should you do if the wheels lock or you need a larger steering adjustment?
choice_a: Release the brakes, then re-apply them as soon as you can
choice_b: Continue pressing the brake pedal as hard as possible
choice_c: Turn off the engine
choice_d: Shift immediately into neutral
explanation: The manual's controlled braking method says to release the brakes if the wheels lock or a larger steering adjustment is needed, then re-apply as soon as possible.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.2, How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: In the "stab braking" method, what should you do as soon as the wheels start rolling again after locking up?
choice_a: Release the brakes completely for the rest of the stop
choice_b: Shift to a higher gear
choice_c: Wait several seconds before doing anything
choice_d: Apply the brakes fully again
explanation: The manual's stab braking method instructs applying the brakes fully again as soon as the wheels start rolling after being released.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.2, Stab Braking

question: If you lose hydraulic brake pressure, what emergency braking option does the manual say is separate from the hydraulic system?
choice_a: The parking (emergency) brake
choice_b: The trailer's electric turn signals
choice_c: The horn
choice_d: The engine's air conditioning compressor
explanation: The manual states the parking or emergency brake is separate from the hydraulic brake system and can be used to slow the vehicle if hydraulic pressure is lost.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.3, Loss of Hydraulic Pressure

question: If your brakes fail on a downgrade and there is no escape ramp available, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Shift into the highest gear to slow the engine
choice_b: Turn off the engine completely and coast
choice_c: Take the least hazardous escape route available, such as an open field or a side road that flattens or turns uphill
choice_d: Continue straight ahead and hope the grade levels out
explanation: The manual advises taking the least hazardous escape route, such as an open field or side road, as soon as you know the brakes don't work, since waiting only makes the vehicle go faster.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.3, Brake Failure on Downgrades

question: If you hear a loud bang while driving, what does the manual advise you to assume?
choice_a: It was probably another vehicle, not yours
choice_b: You should assume it is your own tire that has blown out
choice_c: It is safe to ignore unless the vehicle pulls to one side
choice_d: It is definitely a backfiring engine
explanation: The manual advises that anytime you hear a tire blow, you'd be safest to assume it is yours, since it can take a few seconds for the vehicle to react.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.4, Recognize Tire Failure

question: Immediately after a tire fails, what does the manual say you should do regarding the brake?
choice_a: Pump the brakes rapidly at full speed
choice_b: Brake hard immediately to stop as quickly as possible
choice_c: Stay off the brake until the vehicle has slowed on its own, then brake very gently
choice_d: Apply the parking brake at highway speed
explanation: The manual instructs staying off the brake until the vehicle has slowed, since braking when a tire has failed could cause loss of control, then braking gently and pulling off the road.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.17.4, Respond to Tire Failure

question: What does ABS do, according to the manual's basic description?
choice_a: It keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications
choice_b: It increases the vehicle's maximum braking power
choice_c: It automatically applies the parking brake in an emergency
choice_d: It shortens stopping distance in all conditions
explanation: The manual defines ABS as a computerized system that keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications; it does not increase normal braking capability.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.18, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: As of the manual's stated requirements, truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date must have ABS?
choice_a: March 1, 1996
choice_b: March 1, 1997
choice_c: March 1, 1998
choice_d: March 1, 1999
explanation: The manual states the Department of Transportation requires ABS on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.18.2, Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 pounds or more built on or after what date must have ABS?
choice_a: March 1, 1997
choice_b: March 1, 2000
choice_c: March 1, 1999
choice_d: March 1, 1998
explanation: The manual states hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 pounds or more built on or after March 1, 1999 require ABS.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.18.2, Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: Where are ABS malfunction lamps located on a trailer, according to the manual?
choice_a: On the dashboard only
choice_b: Underneath the trailer only, hidden from view
choice_c: On the left side, either on the front or rear corner
choice_d: There is no lamp for trailers
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.18.3, How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: If only the tractor has ABS in a combination vehicle, what should you watch for while braking?
choice_a: The tractor's fuel gauge dropping suddenly
choice_b: Nothing different than usual
choice_c: The trailer's turn signals malfunctioning
choice_d: The trailer beginning to swing out, and let up on the brakes if it does
explanation: The manual states that when only the tractor has ABS, you should keep an eye on the trailer and let up on the brakes if it begins to swing out.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.18.5, ABS on the Tractor Only or Only on the Trailer

question: According to the manual, what is the one exception that allows a driver to fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop?
choice_a: There is never an exception; always brake gradually
choice_b: Driving in fog with fog lights on
choice_c: Driving downhill in any vehicle
choice_d: Driving a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles
explanation: The manual states the one exception to normal ABS braking procedure is that a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles can be fully braked in an emergency stop.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.18.6, Braking with ABS

question: Which of the following does the manual say ABS will NOT prevent?
choice_a: Wheel lockup during hard braking
choice_b: Loss of control from over braking on ice
choice_c: Power or turning skids caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn
choice_d: Brake-induced skids from over braking
explanation: The manual states ABS won't prevent power or turning skids, which are caused by spinning the drive wheels or excessive speed in a turn, not by over braking.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.18.8, Safety Reminders

question: Which of the following is listed as one of the four causes of a skid?
choice_a: Over-steering, turning the wheels more sharply than the vehicle can turn
choice_b: Using the headlights on high beam
choice_c: Driving with a properly inflated spare tire
choice_d: Signaling too early before a turn
explanation: The manual lists over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast as the four causes of a skid.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.19, Skid Control and Recovery

question: According to the manual, what is the most common type of skid?
choice_a: A front-wheel skid caused by worn steering tires
choice_b: A skid caused by over-inflated tires
choice_c: A skid caused only by high winds
choice_d: A drive-wheel (rear-wheel) skid from excessive braking or acceleration
explanation: The manual states the most common skid is one in which the rear wheels lose traction through excessive braking or acceleration.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.19.1, Drive-wheel Skids

question: In a vehicle towing a trailer, what can a drive-wheel braking skid lead to?
choice_a: Increased fuel efficiency
choice_b: A sudden jackknife, as the trailer pushes the towing vehicle sideways
choice_c: Automatic activation of the parking brake
choice_d: No real danger, since trailers rarely skid
explanation: The manual explains that with vehicles towing trailers, a drive-wheel skid can let the trailer push the towing vehicle sideways, causing a sudden jackknife.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.19.1, Drive-wheel Skids

question: What are the two key actions to correct a drive-wheel braking skid, according to the manual?
choice_a: Shift into a higher gear and brake gently
choice_b: Accelerate hard and steer straight ahead
choice_c: Apply the parking brake and turn on the hazard flashers
choice_d: Stop braking to let the rear wheels roll again, and countersteer
explanation: The manual instructs stopping braking to let the rear wheels roll again, then countersteering as the vehicle straightens out.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.19.2, Correcting a Drive-wheel Braking Skid

question: In a front-wheel skid, what is the only way to stop the skid, according to the manual?
choice_a: Shift into neutral and coast at the same speed
choice_b: Apply full engine power to regain traction
choice_c: Turn the steering wheel harder in the direction of the skid
choice_d: Let the vehicle slow down by easing off the brake and/or steering input
explanation: The manual states that in a front-wheel skid, the only way to stop the skid is to let the vehicle slow down, so you should stop turning and/or braking so hard.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.19.3, Front-wheel Skids

question: What are the three basic steps to take at any accident scene, according to the manual?
choice_a: Assess blame, file a report, contact a lawyer
choice_b: Call your dispatcher, take photographs, exchange insurance information
choice_c: Move all vehicles immediately, block traffic, wait for police
choice_d: Protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured
explanation: The manual lists protecting the area, notifying authorities, and caring for the injured as the basic steps at any accident.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.20, Accident Procedures

question: According to the manual, when should you avoid moving a severely injured person at an accident scene?
choice_a: Unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary
choice_b: Only if a police officer gives permission
choice_c: You should always move them regardless of the situation
choice_d: Moving injured persons is never appropriate under any circumstance
explanation: The manual states not to move a severely injured person unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.20.3, Care for the Injured

question: How does the manual say you should try to stop heavy bleeding from an accident victim's wound?
choice_a: Elevate the wound above the heart only, without pressure
choice_b: Wrap the wound tightly with a tourniquet as a first step
choice_c: Wash the wound thoroughly with water before anything else
choice_d: Apply direct pressure to the wound
explanation: The manual instructs stopping heavy bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.20.3, Care for the Injured

question: Which of the following is listed by the manual as a cause of vehicle fires related to tires?
choice_a: Under-inflated tires and duals that touch
choice_b: Tires rotated too frequently
choice_c: New tires with deep tread
choice_d: Overinflated tires only
explanation: The manual lists under-inflated tires and duals that touch as causes of tire-related vehicle fires.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.21.1, Causes of Fire

question: If your vehicle catches fire, why does the manual specifically advise against pulling into a service station?
choice_a: The presence of fuel at a service station creates additional fire danger
choice_b: Service stations are always closed at night
choice_c: Service stations do not have fire extinguishers
choice_d: It is illegal to stop at a service station in an emergency
explanation: The manual instructs pulling off the road into an open area away from buildings and specifically warns "Don't pull into a service station!" due to the fire hazard from fuel present there.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.21.3, Pull Off the Road

question: For a cargo fire inside a van or box trailer, what does the manual advise regarding the doors?
choice_a: Keep the doors shut, since opening them supplies oxygen and can make the fire burn faster
choice_b: Open the doors immediately to let smoke escape
choice_c: It doesn't matter whether the doors are open or closed
choice_d: Remove one door only, leaving the other closed
explanation: The manual instructs keeping the doors shut on a cargo fire, especially with hazardous materials, since opening them supplies oxygen and can cause the fire to burn very fast.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.21.3, Keep the Fire from Spreading

question: Where should you aim a fire extinguisher when fighting a fire, according to the manual?
choice_a: Directly at any bystanders to keep them back
choice_b: Up into the flames themselves
choice_c: At the top of the vehicle
choice_d: At the source or base of the fire
explanation: The manual instructs aiming the extinguisher at the source or base of the fire, not up into the flames.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.21.3, Extinguish the Fire

question: According to the manual, why should you never use water on an electrical fire?
choice_a: Water evaporates too quickly to be useful
choice_b: Water is too heavy to carry in a fire extinguisher
choice_c: Water can cause an electric shock
choice_d: Water damages the vehicle's paint
explanation: The manual warns that water should not be used on an electrical fire because it can cause shock.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.21.3, Use the Right Fire Extinguisher

question: The manual states a B:C type fire extinguisher is designed to work on which types of fires?
choice_a: Only cargo fires involving hazardous materials
choice_b: Wood, paper, and cloth only
choice_c: Combustible metal fires only
choice_d: Electrical fires and burning liquids
explanation: The manual states the B:C type fire extinguisher is designed to work on electrical fires and burning liquids.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.21.3, Use the Right Fire Extinguisher

question: According to the manual's fire class chart, what type of fire involves wood, paper, and ordinary combustibles?
choice_a: Class C
choice_b: Class D
choice_c: Class B
choice_d: Class A
explanation: The manual's fire class chart identifies Class A as wood, paper, and ordinary combustibles, extinguished by cooling and quenching with water or dry chemicals.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.21.3, Figure 2.20, Class/Type of Fires

question: When using a fire extinguisher, where should you try to position yourself relative to the fire and the wind?
choice_a: Position does not matter
choice_b: Upwind, so the wind carries the extinguisher agent toward the fire
choice_c: Downwind, so the smoke blows toward you for visibility
choice_d: Directly above the fire
explanation: The manual instructs positioning yourself upwind and letting the wind carry the extinguisher agent to the fire.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.21.3, Extinguish the Fire

question: According to the manual, what three factors determine Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC)?
choice_a: Age, gender, and driving experience only
choice_b: Type of alcohol, brand name, and price
choice_c: Amount of alcohol consumed, how fast you drink it, and your body weight
choice_d: Time of day, road conditions, and vehicle size
explanation: The manual states BAC is determined by the amount of alcohol consumed, how fast it is consumed, and the drinker's body weight.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.22.1, What Determines Blood Alcohol Concentration?

question: Which part of the brain does alcohol affect first, according to the manual?
choice_a: The part controlling judgment and self-control
choice_b: The part controlling hearing
choice_c: The part controlling long-term memory
choice_d: The part controlling vision only
explanation: The manual states the first part of the brain affected by alcohol controls judgment and self-control, which can keep drinkers from realizing they are getting drunk.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.22.1, Alcohol and the Brain

question: About how much alcohol can the liver process per hour, according to the manual?
choice_a: One full standard drink per hour
choice_b: About one-third of an ounce per hour
choice_c: Two standard drinks per hour
choice_d: There is no limit; the liver adapts to intake
explanation: The manual states the liver can only process about one-third an ounce of alcohol per hour, which is less than the alcohol in a standard drink, so only time can sober a person up.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.22.1, How Alcohol Works

question: Which of the following drinks contains roughly the same amount of alcohol as a 12-ounce glass of 5% beer, per the manual?
choice_a: A 12-ounce glass of non-alcoholic beer
choice_b: A 12-ounce glass of soda water
choice_c: A 5-ounce glass of 12% wine
choice_d: A 5-ounce cup of coffee
explanation: The manual states a 12-ounce glass of 5% beer, a 5-ounce glass of 12% wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor all contain the same amount of alcohol.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.22.1, What Is a Drink?

question: According to the manual, when is a driver permitted to use a drug prescribed by a doctor while driving?
choice_a: Never, all prescription drugs are prohibited for commercial drivers
choice_b: Only if the motor carrier's insurance approves it in writing
choice_c: Only if the doctor informs the driver it will not affect safe driving ability
choice_d: Only if the drug is taken at night, before sleeping
explanation: The manual states possession and use of a doctor-prescribed drug is permitted if the doctor informs the driver it will not affect safe driving ability.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.22.2, Other Drugs

question: What does the manual say about combining alcohol with other drugs?
choice_a: There is no documented interaction between alcohol and other drugs
choice_b: It is only dangerous if done while driving at night
choice_c: Alcohol can make the effects of other drugs much worse
choice_d: Combining them cancels out most negative effects
explanation: The manual warns that alcohol can make the effects of other drugs much worse, and the safest rule is not to mix drugs with driving at all.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.22.2, Other Drugs

topic: Staying Alert and Fit to Drive
question: About how many hours of sleep does the average person need every 24 hours, according to the manual?
choice_a: 9 to 10 hours
choice_b: 7 to 8 hours
choice_c: 4 to 5 hours
choice_d: 5 to 6 hours
explanation: The manual states the average person needs seven or eight hours of sleep every 24 hours.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.23.1, Get Enough Sleep

topic: Staying Alert and Fit to Drive
question: What does the manual say about "sleep debt"?
choice_a: It has no real physical effect on driving performance
choice_b: It can be paid off only by sleeping; willpower or time alone won't remove it
choice_c: It can be saved up in advance like a bank account
choice_d: It can be eliminated with a strong cup of coffee
explanation: The manual explains that sleep debt can only be paid off by sleeping; you can't overcome it with willpower, and it won't go away by itself.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.23.1, Get Enough Sleep

topic: Staying Alert and Fit to Drive
question: During what hours does the manual say many heavy motor vehicle accidents occur due to driver fatigue?
choice_a: 6 a.m. to noon
choice_b: Noon to 6 p.m.
choice_c: Midnight to 6 a.m.
choice_d: 6 p.m. to midnight
explanation: The manual states many heavy motor vehicle accidents occur between midnight and 6 a.m., when tired drivers can easily fall asleep.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.23.1, Schedule Trips Safely

topic: Staying Alert and Fit to Drive
question: About how long is a typical "micro sleep" that a drowsy driver might experience?
choice_a: About 4 to 5 seconds
choice_b: About 1 full minute
choice_c: About 15 to 20 seconds
choice_d: Less than 1 second
explanation: The manual describes micro sleeps as brief naps that last around four or five seconds, which at 55 mph covers more than 100 yards.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.23.2, Recognize the Danger Signals of Drowsy Driving

topic: Staying Alert and Fit to Drive
question: Which of the following is listed by the manual as a danger signal of drowsy driving?
choice_a: You don't remember driving the last few miles
choice_b: You have the radio on at a moderate volume
choice_c: Consistently checking your mirrors every few seconds
choice_d: You are driving exactly at the speed limit
explanation: The manual lists not remembering driving the last few miles as a danger signal that you may be about to fall asleep.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.23.2, Recognize the Danger Signals of Drowsy Driving

topic: Staying Alert and Fit to Drive
question: According to the manual, what does a half-hour nap do compared to a half-hour coffee stop?
choice_a: Neither has any effect on fatigue
choice_b: They have exactly the same effect
choice_c: It does more to overcome fatigue than a half-hour coffee stop
choice_d: It does less to overcome fatigue than coffee
explanation: The manual states a nap as short as a half-hour will do more to overcome fatigue than a half-hour coffee stop.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.23.3, Take a Nap

topic: Staying Alert and Fit to Drive
question: What does the manual say about using drugs to overcome tiredness while driving?
choice_a: Certain stimulant drugs can safely substitute for sleep
choice_b: Any legal over-the-counter stimulant is acceptable
choice_c: There are no drugs that can overcome being tired; you may end up even more tired afterward
choice_d: Caffeine pills are an approved substitute for rest
explanation: The manual states there are no drugs that can overcome being tired, and you will eventually be even more tired than if you hadn't taken them at all.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.23.3, Avoid Drugs

topic: Staying Alert and Fit to Drive
question: If you become too ill to operate a motor vehicle safely, what does the manual say you should do?
choice_a: Drive only on local roads, avoiding highways
choice_b: Continue driving carefully at reduced speed
choice_c: You must not drive, except that in an emergency you may drive to the nearest place you can safely stop
choice_d: Ask a passenger without a CDL to take over driving
explanation: The manual states that if you become too ill to drive safely, you must not drive, but in an emergency you may drive to the nearest place where you can safely stop.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.23.4, Illness

question: According to the manual, what are hazardous materials?
choice_a: Any cargo weighing more than 10,000 pounds
choice_b: Products that pose a risk to health, safety, and property during transportation
choice_c: Any cargo requiring refrigeration
choice_d: Only cargo that is flammable
explanation: The manual defines hazardous materials as products that pose a risk to health, safety, and property during transportation.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.24.1, What Are Hazardous Materials?

question: What are the three intents of the hazardous materials rules, according to the manual?
choice_a: Increase cargo capacity, reduce fuel use, extend tire life
choice_b: Track GPS location, log driving hours, monitor speed
choice_c: Reduce shipping costs, speed up delivery, simplify paperwork
choice_d: Contain the product, communicate the risk, ensure safe drivers and equipment
explanation: The manual states the intent of hazmat rules is to contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.24.2, Why Are There Rules?

question: According to the manual, how many identical placards must a placarded vehicle display, and where?
choice_a: At least four identical placards, on the front, rear, and both sides
choice_b: One placard, wherever is most visible
choice_c: Two placards, on the front and rear only
choice_d: Six placards, three per side
explanation: The manual states a placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards, placed on the front, rear, and both sides, readable from all four directions.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.24.3, Lists of Regulated Products

question: What letters precede a hazardous materials identification number, according to the manual?
choice_a: DOT or FMCSA
choice_b: NA or UN
choice_c: HM or CD
choice_d: CDL or HZ
explanation: The manual states identification numbers are preceded by the letters "NA" or "UN" and are listed in the US DOT Emergency Response Guidebook.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.24.3, Lists of Regulated Products

question: According to the manual, when is a driver required to have a hazardous materials endorsement to operate a vehicle carrying hazmat cargo?
choice_a: A hazmat endorsement is never required for any driver
choice_b: Whenever the vehicle requires placards
choice_c: Only if the cargo is radioactive
choice_d: Only if the cargo exceeds 5,000 pounds
explanation: The manual states you cannot drive a vehicle requiring placards unless your license has the hazardous materials endorsement; driving one without it is a crime.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.24.3, Lists of Regulated Products

question: According to the manual, a tank endorsement is required if a vehicle carries a portable tank with what minimum capacity?
choice_a: 1,000 gallons or more
choice_b: 500 gallons or more
choice_c: 5,000 gallons or more
choice_d: 100 gallons or more
explanation: The manual states a tank endorsement is required if a vehicle needing a Class A or B CDL carries a portable tank with a capacity of 1,000 gallons or more, or has any permanently mounted cargo tank.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.24.3, Lists of Regulated Products

question: Where must a driver keep hazardous materials shipping papers, according to the manual?
choice_a: In a pouch on the driver's door, in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle
choice_b: In the glove compartment, out of sight
choice_c: Mailed to the motor carrier's office before the trip
choice_d: Locked in the cargo compartment with the hazardous materials
explanation: The manual requires shipping papers to be kept in a pouch on the driver's door, in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when the driver is out of the vehicle.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Subsection 2.24.2, To Communicate the Risk
